log.text: You are born on April 6, 2026, in Georgia.
Your mother, Isabella Davis, is 27. Your father, John, is 25 and does not live with you. You are Isabella's first child. Isabella works, and manages the rest alone.
Ten months old, you take your first steps across the kitchen floor.
Your first year. This was the year you stood up and walked. Most of the year goes on eating, sleeping and getting bigger.
Isabella leaves you with a neighbor before her shift and collects you after it. There is a room that is only yours, and a shelf of books you cannot read yet.
Age 1. You grow out of everything you own, twice.
The flu. You sleep through most of a week and wake up hungry.
Age 2. Most of the year goes on eating, sleeping and getting bigger. Apart from a bout of flu, you were well.
You ask why about everything. The first four answers are patient. The refrigerator is always full. You will be much older before you learn that this is not true of every house.
Age 3. The pencil marks on the door frame move up another two inches.
Age 4. You grow again; last year's shoes no longer fit.
September. You start kindergarten at Sunnyside Elementary, with a backpack that reaches the backs of your knees. Your teacher is Ms. Delgado.
You have a new sister, Lily, born in September.
Age 5. The family grew by one this year. You are taller by the end of the year, and stronger, and hungry most of the time.
Kindergarten gives remarks more than grades. Yours say you are where you should be, or past it.
Age 6. You are faster than you were a year ago, and you can reach the next shelf up.
Your report card is lopsided: B+ in reading and writing, B- in math.
Age 7. The pencil marks on the door frame move up another two inches.
Reading and writing comes easily this year (A-); math does not (C).
Your mother is laid off in June. The talk at dinner turns to what can be put off.
A sheet goes round at school for the track team. Training is most days after class.
You sign up. By the third practice your legs ache in a way that feels like progress.
Your mother finds work again in February. The house loosens.
Age 8. It was a year of worry about money at home. You have more wind than you did a year ago; serious training is the reason.
Third grade ends the way most of your school years do: A- in math, B- in reading and writing.
Age 9. You are fitter than you were twelve months ago, and serious training did it.
Your grades are up this year: A in reading and writing, B+ in math.
Your sister Grace is born in July. At 10, you are old enough to be handed the baby and left with her.
Isabella loses her job. There is no second wage in the house to fall back on, and you can tell.
Age 10. The family grew by one this year. You grow again; last year's shoes no longer fit.
Your grades slip in fifth grade: B+ in reading and writing, B+ in math.
Isabella starts a new job. Nobody says how worried they had been until it is over.
You start at Ridgeview Middle School. Everyone is suddenly sorted into people you sit with and people you do not.
Age 11. A new school this year, and a new set of faces. You are taller by the end of the year, and stronger, and hungry most of the time.
Sixth grade ends. B in reading and writing and B- in math.
Your mother is laid off in September. The talk at dinner turns to what can be put off.
Isabella starts a new job. Nobody says how worried they had been until it is over.
Age 12. A wage stopped coming in this year, and you learned what the adults sound like when they are frightened. You are faster than you were a year ago, and you can reach the next shelf up.
Report card for seventh grade: B+ in reading and writing, B in math.
Age 13. You grow in bursts this year, and your coordination takes a while to catch up.
Eighth grade ends the way most of your school years do: B+ in reading and writing, B+ in math.
High school: Lakeview High School. Grades count from here, and everyone keeps saying so.
Age 14. This was the year high school began. You are stronger than you were last year without having done much to earn it.
Ninth grade ends. B+ in reading and writing and B+ in math.
You have a new sister, Camila, born in February.
Age 15. The family grew by one this year. Your body is still filling out; you are quicker and can go for longer.
Isabella loses her job. There is no second wage in the house to fall back on, and you can tell.
Your mother finds work again in May. The house loosens.
Your report card is lopsided: A- in reading and writing, B+ in math.
The SAT is being given at your school this month. Most colleges that want a score want this one.
Age 16. It was a year of worry about money at home. You are stronger than you were last year without having done much to earn it.
You do not take the SAT.
Top marks again in eleventh grade: A- in reading and writing, B+ in math.
College applications are due this autumn. You have a 3.42 average and no test score. How widely you apply is up to you; each application costs a fee and several evenings.
Four applications go out, a few days before the deadlines.
You are admitted to North Calder State University.
An envelope from Thornfield University: you are in.
Marchetti University says yes.

log.text: Vane University says no.
The answers are in: three of four said yes. You have until the end of May. The figure beside each choice is what a year would cost you after grants and after what your parents can give.
Age 17. A year of forms, essays and waiting for envelopes. You grow in bursts this year, and your coordination takes a while to catch up.
You accept the place at Marchetti University. A year will cost $48,000 after grants; your parents can cover $20,900 of it.
You turn eighteen. On paper you are an adult now: you can vote, sign a lease, and be held to what you sign.
Report card for twelfth grade: A- in math, B in reading and writing.
You graduate from Lakeview High School in June with a 3.40 average. In September you start at Marchetti University.
You sign your first student loan, $5,500, on a web page that takes four minutes to complete.
You start at Marchetti University with fewer classes than most and a job that takes the rest of your week. $18,000 of the year's cost is still not covered.
Marchetti University asks you to declare a field of study. It can be changed later, at a cost in time.
